attempts.answer:
Overview and question framing
Educational technology policy communities have developed numerous teacher digital competence frameworks over the past decade, yet they diverge on whether “content creation” (producing and revising digital artifacts and resources) should be treated as a first‑order, standalone competency or as an embedded capability exercised within pedagogical practice. Examples include the European DigCompEdu, the U.S. ISTE Standards for Educators, and UNESCO’s ICT Competency Framework for Teachers, each with distinct design logics and emphases on how creation relates to pedagogy, subject matter, and professional context. These differences stem from competing epistemologies (skills vs. pedagogy-first vs. integrationist), structural choices in taxonomies, policy contexts (access vs. quality/innovation), and empirical realities of classroom practice and resource ecosystems. <cite id="bc7deb81-0">International frameworks such as ISTE standards, DigCompEdu, UNESCO ICT-CFT, and TPACK have shaped how educators conceptualize digital capability</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-1">Multiple models emphasize technology integration for learning, with TPACK providing a widely adopted integrationist account but criticized for vague boundaries</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE, DigCompEdu, and UNESCO ICT-CFT differ in organization (characteristics, competence areas, and levels), influencing whether creation appears as a standalone competency or embedded within broader categories</cite>.

Conceptual traditions: skills-first, pedagogy-first, and integrationist views
A core source of disagreement is philosophical: whether digital competence is primarily technical skill, primarily pedagogical design, or the integrated orchestration of technology, pedagogy, and content. UNESCO’s ICT-CFT family exemplifies a skills- and access-oriented approach: competencies are organized hierarchically (from knowledge acquisition to knowledge creation) and explicitly include managing, protecting, and sharing digital resources, which places creation as a capability situated within broader professional use, rather than as an autonomous pedagogical domain. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT organizes competencies into levels that culminate in knowledge creation and specifies aspects like managing, protecting, and sharing</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-1">UNESCO’s framework positions teachers’ digital competence as proficiency in using ICT in professional contexts</cite>. By contrast, ISTE Standards for Educators articulate cross‑cutting “characteristics” that teachers should demonstrate (e.g., digital citizenship, creative communication and publication), allowing content creation to surface as an attribute of professionalism and digital practice rather than as a distinct competence area, which can blur its separation from pedagogy. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE comprises seven characteristics with associated actions, situating creation within professional demonstration of competence</cite>. The European DigCompEdu adopts an integrationist stance: it aligns with TPACK and explicitly aims to show how general technological competence and subject-specific pedagogy can be pedagogically integrated to yield inclusive, personalized, innovative learning—hence embedding creation within design/teaching/assessment cycles rather than elevating it to a top-level, autonomous competency. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu agrees with TPACK’s integration thesis and focuses on how technological competence and subject-specific teaching competence can be pedagogically integrated to provide effective, inclusive, personalised and innovative learning</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">At C1–C2 levels, teachers share expertise, experiment with technologies, and develop pedagogical approaches, illustrating integrated professional practice</cite>.

Structural logics: how creation is operationalized
Differences in framework structure produce different answers to the “standalone vs embedded” question. DigCompEdu partitions competencies into six areas with levels A1–C2, using descriptors that include creating and sharing resources as concrete actions within broader pedagogical focus areas. <cite id="bc7deb81-3">Levels 2–5 of the EU framework detail creating/modifying and sharing resources as core pedagogical actions, with levels 2–5 framed as the core pedagogical framework for effective, public strategies</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-3">Level 2 includes “creating and sharing digital resources,” detailing selecting, creating/ modifying, and managing, protecting, and sharing</cite>. DigCompEdu’s design thus embeds creation within the cycle of planning, teaching, assessing, and empowering students’ digital competence. <cite id="bc7deb81-3">Areas 2–5 focus on designing, implementing, and assessing with digital tools, while area 6 targets improving students’ digital competence, including meaningful communication and content creation</cite>. ISTE’s characteristic-based model similarly embeds creation within professionalism and digital practices, as teachers exercise skills like creative communication and publication across instructional contexts. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE defines seven characteristics that teachers should demonstrate, each with actions, rather than isolating content creation as a separate competence area</cite>. Conversely, UNESCO ICT-CFT’s three-tier model foregrounds a progression culminating in knowledge creation, making creation explicit as a professional outcome while keeping it adjacent to knowledge deepening rather than as a first-order, subject‑agnostic competency. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT organizes 18 competencies into Knowledge Acquisition, Knowledge Deepening, Knowledge Creation, with aspects like managing and sharing</cite>. National frameworks mirror these logics: some isolate management or security as independent dimensions (e.g., UNESCO), while others embed creation within pedagogical dimensions, leading to inconsistent treatment across jurisdictions. <cite id="afd98f37-1">The Colombian framework presents research with creativity and innovation as descriptors; management appears as an independent dimension in UNESCO ICT-CFT and in Chilean and Colombian frameworks, while other frameworks do not isolate it</cite><cite id="afd98f37-1">Despite differences, all frameworks retain a pedagogical dimension linking digital technologies to supporting student learning</cite>.

Policy and contextual drivers: access, quality, and assessment imperatives
Policy priorities also drive whether creation is separated or integrated. UNESCO-oriented frameworks often originate in contexts where teacher access, basic ICT mastery, and safe, effective use are primary needs; their tiered model culminating in “knowledge creation” tends to position creation as an advanced, professionalized capability layered onto foundational skills. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-0">UNESCO’s ICT-CFT has been widely adopted in many countries and provides guidelines for essential knowledge and skills for teachers</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT’s levels progress from acquisition to creation, reflecting structured professional development needs</cite>. EU policy emphasizes teacher assessment and school-wide digitalization, so DigCompEdu elevates pedagogical integration and assessment of learning designs, embedding creation within the teacher’s professional pedagogy to ensure quality and inclusion. <cite id="bc7deb81-3">Levels 4–6 build evaluation and feedback while emphasizing engagement, personalization, and students’ responsible creation, underscoring embedded pedagogical oversight</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu’s focus is clearly on pedagogical integration to deliver inclusive, personalized, and innovative experiences</cite>. In contrast, U.S. state adoptions of ISTE emphasize a broad, cross‑sector professional profile; creation appears as a competency attribute of professional practice rather than a distinct domain, reflecting national priorities of systemic alignment and digital citizenship. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE has been adopted across all U.S. states and many countries, outlining characteristics and actions</cite>. These contrasting emphases help explain why some frameworks explicitly list “digital content creation” as a named competence (e.g., in DigComp or national derivatives) while others keep it embedded in pedagogy/security/management dimensions. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-1">The DigComp framework includes content creation as a general digital competence, framed as generating and refining digital content with attention to licensing and clear instructions</cite><cite id="afd98f37-1">Some frameworks identify “digital content creation” as a distinct competency, while others integrate it into broader dimensions</cite>.

Empirical realities: competence gaps, disciplinary variation, and integration needs
Empirical studies report low competence in content creation and call for explicit integration of didactic and relational aspects, reinforcing the view that creation is not merely technical but pedagogically embedded. <cite id="bc7deb81-4">Studies using DigCompEdu found low competence in content creation and problem solving among pre‑service teachers, and highlighted the need to purposefully incorporate relational and didactic aspects of technology integration</cite>. Comparative reviews of national frameworks show that while content creation appears explicitly in some models, most frameworks retain a core pedagogical dimension linking digital tools to student learning, suggesting hybrid positioning where creation is both a taught capability and an applied practice. <cite id="afd98f37-1">Frameworks vary in dimension labels; however, the pedagogical dimension is common, emphasizing teachers’ ability to use digital technologies to support student learning</cite>. The integrationist TPACK tradition, though widely used, has been critiqued for unclear boundaries across knowledge domains; newer EU-oriented frameworks attempt to remedy this by specifying pedagogical foci and progression, which can lead to embedding creation within classroom design and assessment rather than isolating it. <cite id="bc7deb81-1">TPACK has greatly contributed to integrating technology into classrooms but lacks a clear conceptualization of digital literacy and shows vague boundaries across knowledge areas</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu explicitly aims to identify pedagogical and professional focus areas for integrating technology, addressing TPACK’s gaps</cite>. Finally, national implementations often blend frameworks, producing hybrid profiles; for example, Estonia’s standards combine DigCompEdu and ISTE elements, situating creation as part of a broader, cross‑cutting professional profile rather than a standalone axis. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-0">Estonia’s national standards combine DigCompEdu and ISTE, exemplifying hybridization</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-3">ISTE standards can be operationalized via TPACK lesson planning, intertwining content, pedagogy, and tools</cite>.

Why the disagreement persists
- Different epistemologies of digital competence: skills-first models prioritize mastery and safe use before creation; pedagogy-first models treat creation as a professional disposition; integrationist models treat creation as an application of pedagogical and content knowledge, hence embedded in design/teach/assess cycles. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu aligns with TPACK’s integration thesis and embeds creation within pedagogical practice</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE organizes competencies by cross-cutting characteristics rather than isolating creation</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT includes knowledge creation as a final level, tying creation to progression</cite>.
- Divergent policy goals and contexts: access and foundational skills drive UNESCO-like models that scaffold creation onto core competencies; systemic quality and inclusion drive EU models that embed creation within pedagogical design and assessment; national adoption and broad sector applicability drive ISTE’s cross-cutting attributes. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-0">UNESCO and DigCompEdu inform national frameworks; Estonia and Ireland blend approaches</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-3">EU levels emphasize evaluation, personalization, and students’ responsible creation, reflecting inclusion and quality</cite>.
- Evidence of practice: low competence in creation and the need to integrate didactic/relational aspects argue for embedding creation within pedagogy rather than treating it as a purely technical specialty; critiques of TPACK’s boundary vagueness motivate frameworks to operationalize creation in concrete pedagogical actions and progressions. <cite id="bc7deb81-4">Empirical findings of low content-creation competence and calls for integrating relational/didactic aspects</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-1">Critiques of TPACK’s discrimination and boundary vagueness</cite>.
- Practical affordances and constraints: creation involves legal/ethical/licensing, accessibility, and instructional quality, which are not purely technical; EU frameworks explicitly call out licensing and clarity, aligning with pedagogical responsibility, while national frameworks may isolate management/security to emphasize risk and quality control. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-1">Digital content creation includes generating/refining content with attention to copyright/licensing and clear instructions</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO includes management, protection, and sharing as aspects adjacent to creation</cite>.

Toward convergence and hybridization
Comparative reviews show an emerging convergence: many frameworks now explicitly include “digital content creation” yet also maintain a strong pedagogical dimension, with some national profiles treating creation as a core dimension and others as a descriptor of pedagogy. <cite id="afd98f37-1">Some frameworks identify digital content creation as a distinct competence, while others integrate it into pedagogical dimensions common to all frameworks</cite>. EU-oriented instruments like DigCompEdu and national hybrids (e.g., Estonia) illustrate how “embedded creation” can be operationalized through staged progressions and professionalized pedagogy, while ISTE’s characteristic model shows how cross-sector adoption can diffuse creation across professional roles. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-0">Estonia’s standards combine DigCompEdu and ISTE, reflecting hybridization</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-3">EU levels and areas frame creation as part of pedagogical practice and student empowerment</cite>. In short, the disagreement reflects underlying tensions between capability lists and professional integration, between foundational access and advanced innovation, and between technical, legal-ethical, and instructional quality concerns—tensions that hybrid frameworks increasingly attempt to reconcile by embedding creation within pedagogy while acknowledging it as a distinct professional outcome. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu’s explicit focus on pedagogical integration addresses TPACK’s gaps</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO and ISTE illustrate access-oriented and cross-cutting professionalization, respectively</cite><cite id="afd98f37-1">Across frameworks, the shared pedagogical dimension underscores the integrationist impulse</cite>.

Practical implications for practice and policy
- If your goal is baseline access and safe, legal use, structure creation as a progression within ICT competence (acquisition → deepening → creation) and include licensing, security, and management as adjacent dimensions. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT’s tiered model culminating in knowledge creation</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">Includes managing, protecting, and sharing as aspects</cite>.
- If your goal is classroom quality and inclusion, embed creation within design-teach-assess cycles and tie creation outcomes to student empowerment, accessibility, and formative evaluation. <cite id="bc7deb81-3">Levels 4–6 emphasize evaluation and personalization, with students’ responsible creation</cite>.
- If your goal is broad professional development and systemic adoption, use a cross-cutting model that makes creation a characteristic of professional practice and digital citizenship, operationalized via integrationist design (e.g., TPACK-informed planning). <cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE’s characteristics and actions</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-3">ISTE standards can be instantiated through TPACK lesson planning, integrating content, pedagogy, and tools</cite>.

In sum, frameworks disagree because they answer differently the deeper question: should digital competence be a checklist of capabilities, a professional profile oriented to practice, or an integrated, context‑sensitive orchestration of technology, pedagogy, and content? Each choice yields different placement of content creation—either as a standalone capability to be mastered, as an embedded pedagogical action to be designed and assessed, or as a characteristic of professionalized digital practice. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">Integrationist frameworks like DigCompEdu and TPACK argue that creation is the product of pedagogical and content knowledge</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE and UNESCO models operationalize creation as cross-cutting professional behavior or tiered progression within professional use</cite>.

The DigCompEdu framework proposes a progression model that describes the different stages of digital competence development. These competence stages are expressed as proficiency levels, with A1 corresponding to the lowest and C2 to the highest. The descriptors provided by the framework were used to develop a self-reflection instrument, which is referred to ahead. 

The DigCompEdu framework and its related self-reflection instrument have been increasingly used to examine teachers' digital competence [23,24], but few studies have focused on these competences across different STEM subjects. The few available studies mostly pertain to single curricular subjects, small samples, or other contexts rather than school education. For instance, Rooy [25] concluded that experienced Australian biology teachers do incorporate technologies, however limited, in order to improve the quality of student learning. In Spain, Fraile, Peñalva-Vélez, and Lacambra [26] assessed the competence level of 43 schoolteachers in initial training and found it was low in content creation and problem solving. Those authors also highlighted the urgent need to purposefully incorporate relational and didactic aspects of digital technology integration in teacher education. 

While offering important insights, these studies fail to provide a more nuanced view of how digital competences are perceived by different teachers in STEM areas. Our study draws from a large sample, which constitutes a unique opportunity to focus on the differences across different STEM subjects.

The International Society of Technology in Education (ISTE, 2018) developed the ISTE Standards for Teachers that provides guidelines for essential technology knowledge and skills. Furthermore, several countries have developed National frameworks combining items from more than one framework. For example, Estonia developed the Standards for Learning, Leading and Teaching in the Digital Age based on DigCompEdu and ISTE (2018), while Ireland developed the Digital Learning Framework which is based on DigCompEdu and UNESCO ICT CTF (Eurydice Report, 2019).

Another popular framework concerning the teachers' technological knowledge is the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), proposed by Mishra and Koehler (2006). The framework describes three basic components of knowledge during teaching and learning, namely technology, content, and pedagogy. TPACK describes the three main components of technological knowledge, pedagogical knowledge, and content knowledge as well as four intersectional components, namely, technological content knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, technological pedagogical knowledge, and technological pedagogical content knowledge (e.g., Schmid et al., 2020). Several studies have recently applied and (re)validated TPACK to assess the teachers' digital skills across different teaching stages and domains (e.g., Schmid et al., 2020).

Finally, several researchers used the International Computer Driving License (ICDL, 2018) to assess the teachers' digital competence, or developed web-based tools to efficiently integrate the framework in educational institutions (e.g., Idrizi et al., 2018). ICDL can be applied in any field of occupation and has been widely adopted by many countries and institutions to evaluate a person's knowledge on basic ICT concepts like computer basics, word processing and spreadsheets, typing skills, online essentials, online collaboration, image editing, security, presentation, and database.

Snippet: Three of the seven frameworks included in the analysis, the DigCompEdu framework (Redecker & Punie, 2017), the ISTE Standards for Educators (ISTE, 2019), and the UNESCO ICT Competency Framework for Teachers (UNESCO, 2018), were international frameworks developed for national and regional organisation to use when creating their own PDC frameworks. The DigCompEdu framework, which has been used throughout Europe (Redecker & Punie, 2017), is organised around six competence areas, each of which include three to five specific competencies. Each competence is then broken down to include professional activities and steps for competence progression. The ISTE framework, which has been adopted in all 50 U.S. states, most Canadian provinces, and in many other countries (ISTE, 2019), comprises seven characteristics a digitally competent teacher should demonstrate, and an outline of actions associated with each characteristic. The UNESCO framework, which has been applied in many African, Asian, and Latin American countries (UNESCO, 2018) includes 18 competencies organised into three levels (Knowledge Acquisition, Knowledge Deepening, Knowledge Creation); each level includes six associated aspects of competence. 

The four other frameworks; the Norwegian Professional Digital Competence Framework for Teachers (Kelentrić et al., 2017), the South African Professional Development Framework for Digital Learning (Department of Basic Education [DBE], 2018), the Spanish Common Digital Competence Framework for Teachers (INTEF, 2017), and the UK Digital Teaching Professional Framework (Education and Training Foundation [ETF], 2018); were developed as part of national digital competence efforts in their respective nations. The Norwegian framework includes seven competence areas containing details regarding associated knowledge, skills, and competence. The South African framework is embedded within a larger document outlining teacher professional development needs and digital learning approaches, and contains 13 digital learning competencies connected to the areas of Professional Growth and Knowledge, Curriculum Focus, and Leadership. The Spanish framework includes five competence areas and extensive explanations concerning abilities and proficiency levels within each area. The UK framework is designed for educators working in traditional K-12 school settings and those working in other areas of education, and is organised around aspects of teaching, such as planning, accessibility and inclusion, and teachers' and learners' selfdevelopment.

Overview and question framing
Educational technology policy communities have developed numerous teacher digital competence frameworks over the past decade, yet they diverge on whether “content creation” (producing and revising digital artifacts and resources) should be treated as a first‑order, standalone competency or as an embedded capability exercised within pedagogical practice. Examples include the European DigCompEdu, the U.S. ISTE Standards for Educators, and UNESCO’s ICT Competency Framework for Teachers, each with distinct design logics and emphases on how creation relates to pedagogy, subject matter, and professional context. These differences stem from competing epistemologies (skills vs. pedagogy-first vs. integrationist), structural choices in taxonomies, policy contexts (access vs. quality/innovation), and empirical realities of classroom practice and resource ecosystems. <cite id="bc7deb81-0">International frameworks such as ISTE standards, DigCompEdu, UNESCO ICT-CFT, and TPACK have shaped how educators conceptualize digital capability</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-1">Multiple models emphasize technology integration for learning, with TPACK providing a widely adopted integrationist account but criticized for vague boundaries</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE, DigCompEdu, and UNESCO ICT-CFT differ in organization (characteristics, competence areas, and levels), influencing whether creation appears as a standalone competency or embedded within broader categories</cite>.

Conceptual traditions: skills-first, pedagogy-first, and integrationist views
A core source of disagreement is philosophical: whether digital competence is primarily technical skill, primarily pedagogical design, or the integrated orchestration of technology, pedagogy, and content. UNESCO’s ICT-CFT family exemplifies a skills- and access-oriented approach: competencies are organized hierarchically (from knowledge acquisition to knowledge creation) and explicitly include managing, protecting, and sharing digital resources, which places creation as a capability situated within broader professional use, rather than as an autonomous pedagogical domain. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT organizes competencies into levels that culminate in knowledge creation and specifies aspects like managing, protecting, and sharing</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-1">UNESCO’s framework positions teachers’ digital competence as proficiency in using ICT in professional contexts</cite>. By contrast, ISTE Standards for Educators articulate cross‑cutting “characteristics” that teachers should demonstrate (e.g., digital citizenship, creative communication and publication), allowing content creation to surface as an attribute of professionalism and digital practice rather than as a distinct competence area, which can blur its separation from pedagogy. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE comprises seven characteristics with associated actions, situating creation within professional demonstration of competence</cite>. The European DigCompEdu adopts an integrationist stance: it aligns with TPACK and explicitly aims to show how general technological competence and subject-specific pedagogy can be pedagogically integrated to yield inclusive, personalized, innovative learning—hence embedding creation within design/teaching/assessment cycles rather than elevating it to a top-level, autonomous competency. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu agrees with TPACK’s integration thesis and focuses on how technological competence and subject-specific teaching competence can be pedagogically integrated to provide effective, inclusive, personalised and innovative learning</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">At C1–C2 levels, teachers share expertise, experiment with technologies, and develop pedagogical approaches, illustrating integrated professional practice</cite>.

Structural logics: how creation is operationalized
Differences in framework structure produce different answers to the “standalone vs embedded” question. DigCompEdu partitions competencies into six areas with levels A1–C2, using descriptors that include creating and sharing resources as concrete actions within broader pedagogical focus areas. <cite id="bc7deb81-3">Levels 2–5 of the EU framework detail creating/modifying and sharing resources as core pedagogical actions, with levels 2–5 framed as the core pedagogical framework for effective, public strategies</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-3">Level 2 includes “creating and sharing digital resources,” detailing selecting, creating/ modifying, and managing, protecting, and sharing</cite>. DigCompEdu’s design thus embeds creation within the cycle of planning, teaching, assessing, and empowering students’ digital competence. <cite id="bc7deb81-3">Areas 2–5 focus on designing, implementing, and assessing with digital tools, while area 6 targets improving students’ digital competence, including meaningful communication and content creation</cite>. ISTE’s characteristic-based model similarly embeds creation within professionalism and digital practices, as teachers exercise skills like creative communication and publication across instructional contexts. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE defines seven characteristics that teachers should demonstrate, each with actions, rather than isolating content creation as a separate competence area</cite>. Conversely, UNESCO ICT-CFT’s three-tier model foregrounds a progression culminating in knowledge creation, making creation explicit as a professional outcome while keeping it adjacent to knowledge deepening rather than as a first-order, subject‑agnostic competency. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT organizes 18 competencies into Knowledge Acquisition, Knowledge Deepening, Knowledge Creation, with aspects like managing and sharing</cite>. National frameworks mirror these logics: some isolate management or security as independent dimensions (e.g., UNESCO), while others embed creation within pedagogical dimensions, leading to inconsistent treatment across jurisdictions. <cite id="afd98f37-1">The Colombian framework presents research with creativity and innovation as descriptors; management appears as an independent dimension in UNESCO ICT-CFT and in Chilean and Colombian frameworks, while other frameworks do not isolate it</cite><cite id="afd98f37-1">Despite differences, all frameworks retain a pedagogical dimension linking digital technologies to supporting student learning</cite>.

Policy and contextual drivers: access, quality, and assessment imperatives
Policy priorities also drive whether creation is separated or integrated. UNESCO-oriented frameworks often originate in contexts where teacher access, basic ICT mastery, and safe, effective use are primary needs; their tiered model culminating in “knowledge creation” tends to position creation as an advanced, professionalized capability layered onto foundational skills. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-0">UNESCO’s ICT-CFT has been widely adopted in many countries and provides guidelines for essential knowledge and skills for teachers</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT’s levels progress from acquisition to creation, reflecting structured professional development needs</cite>. EU policy emphasizes teacher assessment and school-wide digitalization, so DigCompEdu elevates pedagogical integration and assessment of learning designs, embedding creation within the teacher’s professional pedagogy to ensure quality and inclusion. <cite id="bc7deb81-3">Levels 4–6 build evaluation and feedback while emphasizing engagement, personalization, and students’ responsible creation, underscoring embedded pedagogical oversight</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu’s focus is clearly on pedagogical integration to deliver inclusive, personalized, and innovative experiences</cite>. In contrast, U.S. state adoptions of ISTE emphasize a broad, cross‑sector professional profile; creation appears as a competency attribute of professional practice rather than a distinct domain, reflecting national priorities of systemic alignment and digital citizenship. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE has been adopted across all U.S. states and many countries, outlining characteristics and actions</cite>. These contrasting emphases help explain why some frameworks explicitly list “digital content creation” as a named competence (e.g., in DigComp or national derivatives) while others keep it embedded in pedagogy/security/management dimensions. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-1">The DigComp framework includes content creation as a general digital competence, framed as generating and refining digital content with attention to licensing and clear instructions</cite><cite id="afd98f37-1">Some frameworks identify “digital content creation” as a distinct competency, while others integrate it into broader dimensions</cite>.

Empirical realities: competence gaps, disciplinary variation, and integration needs
Empirical studies report low competence in content creation and call for explicit integration of didactic and relational aspects, reinforcing the view that creation is not merely technical but pedagogically embedded. <cite id="bc7deb81-4">Studies using DigCompEdu found low competence in content creation and problem solving among pre‑service teachers, and highlighted the need to purposefully incorporate relational and didactic aspects of technology integration</cite>. Comparative reviews of national frameworks show that while content creation appears explicitly in some models, most frameworks retain a core pedagogical dimension linking digital tools to student learning, suggesting hybrid positioning where creation is both a taught capability and an applied practice. <cite id="afd98f37-1">Frameworks vary in dimension labels; however, the pedagogical dimension is common, emphasizing teachers’ ability to use digital technologies to support student learning</cite>. The integrationist TPACK tradition, though widely used, has been critiqued for unclear boundaries across knowledge domains; newer EU-oriented frameworks attempt to remedy this by specifying pedagogical foci and progression, which can lead to embedding creation within classroom design and assessment rather than isolating it. <cite id="bc7deb81-1">TPACK has greatly contributed to integrating technology into classrooms but lacks a clear conceptualization of digital literacy and shows vague boundaries across knowledge areas</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu explicitly aims to identify pedagogical and professional focus areas for integrating technology, addressing TPACK’s gaps</cite>. Finally, national implementations often blend frameworks, producing hybrid profiles; for example, Estonia’s standards combine DigCompEdu and ISTE elements, situating creation as part of a broader, cross‑cutting professional profile rather than a standalone axis. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-0">Estonia’s national standards combine DigCompEdu and ISTE, exemplifying hybridization</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-3">ISTE standards can be operationalized via TPACK lesson planning, intertwining content, pedagogy, and tools</cite>.

Why the disagreement persists
- Different epistemologies of digital competence: skills-first models prioritize mastery and safe use before creation; pedagogy-first models treat creation as a professional disposition; integrationist models treat creation as an application of pedagogical and content knowledge, hence embedded in design/teach/assess cycles. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu aligns with TPACK’s integration thesis and embeds creation within pedagogical practice</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE organizes competencies by cross-cutting characteristics rather than isolating creation</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT includes knowledge creation as a final level, tying creation to progression</cite>.
- Divergent policy goals and contexts: access and foundational skills drive UNESCO-like models that scaffold creation onto core competencies; systemic quality and inclusion drive EU models that embed creation within pedagogical design and assessment; national adoption and broad sector applicability drive ISTE’s cross-cutting attributes. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-0">UNESCO and DigCompEdu inform national frameworks; Estonia and Ireland blend approaches</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-3">EU levels emphasize evaluation, personalization, and students’ responsible creation, reflecting inclusion and quality</cite>.
- Evidence of practice: low competence in creation and the need to integrate didactic/relational aspects argue for embedding creation within pedagogy rather than treating it as a purely technical specialty; critiques of TPACK’s boundary vagueness motivate frameworks to operationalize creation in concrete pedagogical actions and progressions. <cite id="bc7deb81-4">Empirical findings of low content-creation competence and calls for integrating relational/didactic aspects</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-1">Critiques of TPACK’s discrimination and boundary vagueness</cite>.
- Practical affordances and constraints: creation involves legal/ethical/licensing, accessibility, and instructional quality, which are not purely technical; EU frameworks explicitly call out licensing and clarity, aligning with pedagogical responsibility, while national frameworks may isolate management/security to emphasize risk and quality control. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-1">Digital content creation includes generating/refining content with attention to copyright/licensing and clear instructions</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO includes management, protection, and sharing as aspects adjacent to creation</cite>.

Toward convergence and hybridization
Comparative reviews show an emerging convergence: many frameworks now explicitly include “digital content creation” yet also maintain a strong pedagogical dimension, with some national profiles treating creation as a core dimension and others as a descriptor of pedagogy. <cite id="afd98f37-1">Some frameworks identify digital content creation as a distinct competence, while others integrate it into pedagogical dimensions common to all frameworks</cite>. EU-oriented instruments like DigCompEdu and national hybrids (e.g., Estonia) illustrate how “embedded creation” can be operationalized through staged progressions and professionalized pedagogy, while ISTE’s characteristic model shows how cross-sector adoption can diffuse creation across professional roles. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-0">Estonia’s standards combine DigCompEdu and ISTE, reflecting hybridization</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-3">EU levels and areas frame creation as part of pedagogical practice and student empowerment</cite>. In short, the disagreement reflects underlying tensions between capability lists and professional integration, between foundational access and advanced innovation, and between technical, legal-ethical, and instructional quality concerns—tensions that hybrid frameworks increasingly attempt to reconcile by embedding creation within pedagogy while acknowledging it as a distinct professional outcome. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">DigCompEdu’s explicit focus on pedagogical integration addresses TPACK’s gaps</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO and ISTE illustrate access-oriented and cross-cutting professionalization, respectively</cite><cite id="afd98f37-1">Across frameworks, the shared pedagogical dimension underscores the integrationist impulse</cite>.

Practical implications for practice and policy
- If your goal is baseline access and safe, legal use, structure creation as a progression within ICT competence (acquisition → deepening → creation) and include licensing, security, and management as adjacent dimensions. <cite id="bc7deb81-2">UNESCO ICT-CFT’s tiered model culminating in knowledge creation</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">Includes managing, protecting, and sharing as aspects</cite>.
- If your goal is classroom quality and inclusion, embed creation within design-teach-assess cycles and tie creation outcomes to student empowerment, accessibility, and formative evaluation. <cite id="bc7deb81-3">Levels 4–6 emphasize evaluation and personalization, with students’ responsible creation</cite>.
- If your goal is broad professional development and systemic adoption, use a cross-cutting model that makes creation a characteristic of professional practice and digital citizenship, operationalized via integrationist design (e.g., TPACK-informed planning). <cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE’s characteristics and actions</cite><cite id="5dc5e4d7-3">ISTE standards can be instantiated through TPACK lesson planning, integrating content, pedagogy, and tools</cite>.

In sum, frameworks disagree because they answer differently the deeper question: should digital competence be a checklist of capabilities, a professional profile oriented to practice, or an integrated, context‑sensitive orchestration of technology, pedagogy, and content? Each choice yields different placement of content creation—either as a standalone capability to be mastered, as an embedded pedagogical action to be designed and assessed, or as a characteristic of professionalized digital practice. <cite id="5dc5e4d7-2">Integrationist frameworks like DigCompEdu and TPACK argue that creation is the product of pedagogical and content knowledge</cite><cite id="bc7deb81-2">ISTE and UNESCO models operationalize creation as cross-cutting professional behavior or tiered progression within professional use</cite>. </answer>

Title: Validity evidence regarding the use of DigCompEdu as a self-reflection tool: The case of Hungarian teacher educators
Snippet: The literature clearly distinguishes between digital literacy, as an ability to understand and use information presented via computers and digital competence, as proficiency in using ICT in a professional context (Spante et al., 2018). This later notion of digital competence corresponds to the integration of ICT in a daily work setting which follows the concept of professional digital competence: the ability of teachers to work in a digitalized environment (e.g. teaching with digital tools, managing digital learning environments etc.) as defined by Starkey (2020). The concept of professional digital competence signals a shift towards a more complex, context-sensitive understanding of TDC (McDonagh et al., 2021;Siddiq et al., 2024). 

According to Falloon (2020), there are several frameworks and models were built to assess and develop the digital capability of teachers, such as: 

• SAMR (Substitution Augmentation Modification Redefinition) model (Puentedura, 2003). • TPACK (Technological, Pedagogical and Content Knowledge) model (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). • DECK (distributed thinking and knowing, engagement, communication and community, knowledge building) framework (Fisher et al., 2012). • CDL (Critical Digital Literacy) framework (Hinrichsen & Coombs, 2013). 

• TEIL (Teacher Education Information Literacy) framework (Klebansky & Fraser, 2013). • ISTE (International Society for Technology in Education) standards for educators (https:// www. iste. org/ stand ards/ for-educa tors). • Digital Competence of Educators (DigCompEdu) framework (Redecker, 2017). • PIC (passive, interactive, creative) -RAT (replace, amplify, transform) framework (Kimmons et al., 2020). • TDC (Teacher Digital Competence) framework (Falloon, 2020).

Title: Tools for assessing teacher digital literacy: a review
Snippet: Likewise, the Education and Teaching Foundation in Britain designed the Digital Teaching Professional Framework (Education & Training Foundation, 2019) to support educators in understanding technology integration, in cultivating the practice of teaching with technology, and in supplementing their professional development. The framework specifies teacher competence from seven aspects (planning pedagogy, approach pedagogy, student employability, specific teaching, assessment, accessibility and inclusion, and personal development). Each aspect is classified into three levels: exploration, adaptation, and leadership. As regards the seven aspects, the nature of each aspect was relatively consistent with a few international frameworks, such as DigCompEdu and UNESCO ICT-CFT. Moreover, the framework highlighted that the focal point of the competence of educators is to foster learners in using digital technology to enhance their employment and entrepreneurial prospects. 

Multiple models and frameworks from various empirical studies have also contributed to the evaluation of digital literacy in specific educational contexts (e.g., Mishra & Koehler, 2006;Puentedura, 2006). Certain models or frameworks emphasize teacher competence in incorporating technology into the teaching process to enhance learning. Mishra and Koehler (2006) have developed a technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) model that aims to illustrate effective teaching using technology to incorporate technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge. Undeniably, the framework has greatly contributed to integrating technology into the classroom. However, the model is limited because it does not offer a conceptualization of digital literacy for educators. Additionally, scholars have demonstrated the lack of discrimination between different areas of knowledge, while the boundaries of the aspects are vague (Drummond & Sweeney, 2017). Alternatively, the Substitution Augmentation Modification Redefinition (SAMR; Puentedura, 2006) model was developed as a descriptive framework with four levels of hierarchy (substitution, augmentation, modification, and redefinition). It follows the taxonomy from low to high levels and has been widely used by educational researchers and trainers as a guide for teachers in the technology integration process.

Title: Algorithmic futures: an analysis of teacher professional digital competence frameworks through an algorithm literacy lens
Snippet: Three of the seven frameworks included in the analysis, the DigCompEdu framework (Redecker & Punie, 2017), the ISTE Standards for Educators (ISTE, 2019), and the UNESCO ICT Competency Framework for Teachers (UNESCO, 2018), were international frameworks developed for national and regional organisation to use when creating their own PDC frameworks. The DigCompEdu framework, which has been used throughout Europe (Redecker & Punie, 2017), is organised around six competence areas, each of which include three to five specific competencies. Each competence is then broken down to include professional activities and steps for competence progression. The ISTE framework, which has been adopted in all 50 U.S. states, most Canadian provinces, and in many other countries (ISTE, 2019), comprises seven characteristics a digitally competent teacher should demonstrate, and an outline of actions associated with each characteristic. The UNESCO framework, which has been applied in many African, Asian, and Latin American countries (UNESCO, 2018) includes 18 competencies organised into three levels (Knowledge Acquisition, Knowledge Deepening, Knowledge Creation); each level includes six associated aspects of competence. 

The four other frameworks; the Norwegian Professional Digital Competence Framework for Teachers (Kelentrić et al., 2017), the South African Professional Development Framework for Digital Learning (Department of Basic Education [DBE], 2018), the Spanish Common Digital Competence Framework for Teachers (INTEF, 2017), and the UK Digital Teaching Professional Framework (Education and Training Foundation [ETF], 2018); were developed as part of national digital competence efforts in their respective nations. The Norwegian framework includes seven competence areas containing details regarding associated knowledge, skills, and competence. The South African framework is embedded within a larger document outlining teacher professional development needs and digital learning approaches, and contains 13 digital learning competencies connected to the areas of Professional Growth and Knowledge, Curriculum Focus, and Leadership. The Spanish framework includes five competence areas and extensive explanations concerning abilities and proficiency levels within each area. The UK framework is designed for educators working in traditional K-12 school settings and those working in other areas of education, and is organised around aspects of teaching, such as planning, accessibility and inclusion, and teachers' and learners' selfdevelopment.

Title: The Digital Competence of Future Teachers: Self-Assessment in the Context of Their Development
Snippet: In the European context, a framework for teachers' digital competence is developed, targeting educators at all levels of education, from early childhood to higher education and adult education, including vocational training, special education and non-formal learning. It aims to encompass these digital competences specifically for teachers and draws attention to the specific dimensions of digital competency, enabling it to develop its models in European Union countries at national and regional level. 

The proposed framework addresses six different levels of competence with a total of 22 specific competencies. These basic levels are: [23] In order to facilitate the adoption of the framework, the expert levels are presented through a well-defined description of specific roles that can also be projected on the professional levels proposed in the Common European Framework for Foreign Language Skills from A1 to C2 (see Table 1). The training of pedagogical specialists at university level only reaches level B1, which tends to hinder subsequent qualification. This framework requires the development of a comprehensive strategy for the development of the digital competence of teachers guaranteeing quality both within their university education and in the context of continuing qualification of pedagogical specialists through different forms and activities. 

Level 1 focuses on the professional environment and is directly related to professional engagement, which is concretized through: 1) Organizational communication 2) Professional cooperation 3) Professional reflection 4) Continuing professional development in the context of the digital environment Level 2 focuses on creating and sharing digital resources through the possibilities of: 

1) Selecting 2) Creating and modifying 3) Managing, protecting and sharing Level 3 focuses on managing and regulating the use of digital tools in learning and teaching. Level 4 builds on digital tools and strategies to improve evaluation, as well as the analysis of evidence and the realization of complete feedback on evaluation. Level 5 focuses on the use of digital tools to support learning, focusing on their full involvement, engagement, differentiation and personalization. Level 6 is concerned with the improvement of students' digital competence with a focus on their information and media literacy, meaningful communication, content creation, responsible use of information and communication technologies and digital resources, and problem solving through targeted use. Levels 2 through 5 represent the core of the pedagogical framework and they detail teacher competences to create and strengthen effective, publicly accessible and innovative learning strategies through digital tools [23].

Title: STEM Teachers’ Digital Competence: Different Subjects, Different Proficiencies
Snippet: Areas 2 to 5, the core of the framework, detail the pedagogical and methodological aspects specific to the teaching process (designing, implementing, and assessing). Area 1 details the digital competences needed to engage with the professional working environment, and area 6 details the digital competences required to facilitate the development of students' digital competence. 

The DigCompEdu framework proposes a progression model that describes the different stages of digital competence development. These competence stages are expressed as proficiency levels, with A1 corresponding to the lowest and C2 to the highest. For each of the 22 competences, a proficiency descriptor is provided, exemplifying activities at each proficiency level. The descriptors provided by the framework were used to develop a self-reflection instrument, which is referred to ahead. 

The DigCompEdu framework and its related self-reflection instrument have been increasingly used to examine teachers' digital competence [23,24], but few studies have focused on these competences across different STEM subjects. The few available studies mostly pertain to single curricular subjects, small samples, or other contexts rather than school education. For instance, Rooy [25] concluded that experienced Australian biology teachers do incorporate technologies, however limited, in order to improve the quality of student learning. In Spain, Fraile, Peñalva-Vélez, and Lacambra [26] assessed the competence level of 43 schoolteachers in initial training and found it was low in content creation and problem solving. Those authors also highlighted the urgent need to purposefully incorporate relational and didactic aspects of digital technology integration in teacher education. 

While offering important insights, these studies fail to provide a more nuanced view of how digital competences are perceived by different teachers in STEM areas. Our study draws from a large sample, which constitutes a unique opportunity to focus on the differences across different STEM subjects.

It follows the taxonomy from low to high levels and has been widely used by educational researchers and trainers as a guide for teachers in the technology integration process.

documents.title: Algorithmic futures: an analysis of teacher professional digital competence frameworks through an algorithm literacy lens
documents.snippet:
Three of the seven frameworks included in the analysis, the DigCompEdu framework (Redecker & Punie, 2017), the ISTE Standards for Educators (ISTE, 2019), and the UNESCO ICT Competency Framework for Teachers (UNESCO, 2018), were international frameworks developed for national and regional organisation to use when creating their own PDC frameworks. The DigCompEdu framework, which has been used throughout Europe (Redecker & Punie, 2017), is organised around six competence areas, each of which include three to five specific competencies. Each competence is then broken down to include professional activities and steps for competence progression. The ISTE framework, which has been adopted in all 50 U.S. states, most Canadian provinces, and in many other countries (ISTE, 2019), comprises seven characteristics a digitally competent teacher should demonstrate, and an outline of actions associated with each characteristic. The UNESCO framework, which has been applied in many African, Asian, and Latin American countries (UNESCO, 2018) includes 18 competencies organised into three levels (Knowledge Acquisition, Knowledge Deepening, Knowledge Creation); each level includes six associated aspects of competence. 

The four other frameworks; the Norwegian Professional Digital Competence Framework for Teachers (Kelentrić et al., 2017), the South African Professional Development Framework for Digital Learning (Department of Basic Education [DBE], 2018), the Spanish Common Digital Competence Framework for Teachers (INTEF, 2017), and the UK Digital Teaching Professional Framework (Education and Training Foundation [ETF], 2018); were developed as part of national digital competence efforts in their respective nations. The Norwegian framework includes seven competence areas containing details regarding associated knowledge, skills, and competence. The South African framework is embedded within a larger document outlining teacher professional development needs and digital learning approaches, and contains 13 digital learning competencies connected to the areas of Professional Growth and Knowledge, Curriculum Focus, and Leadership. The Spanish framework includes five competence areas and extensive explanations concerning abilities and proficiency levels within each area. The UK framework is designed for educators working in traditional K-12 school settings and those working in other areas of education, and is organised around aspects of teaching, such as planning, accessibility and inclusion, and teachers' and learners' selfdevelopment.

documents.title: The Digital Competence of Future Teachers: Self-Assessment in the Context of Their Development
documents.snippet:
In the European context, a framework for teachers' digital competence is developed, targeting educators at all levels of education, from early childhood to higher education and adult education, including vocational training, special education and non-formal learning. It aims to encompass these digital competences specifically for teachers and draws attention to the specific dimensions of digital competency, enabling it to develop its models in European Union countries at national and regional level. 

The proposed framework addresses six different levels of competence with a total of 22 specific competencies. These basic levels are: [23] In order to facilitate the adoption of the framework, the expert levels are presented through a well-defined description of specific roles that can also be projected on the professional levels proposed in the Common European Framework for Foreign Language Skills from A1 to C2 (see Table 1). The training of pedagogical specialists at university level only reaches level B1, which tends to hinder subsequent qualification. This framework requires the development of a comprehensive strategy for the development of the digital competence of teachers guaranteeing quality both within their university education and in the context of continuing qualification of pedagogical specialists through different forms and activities. 

Level 1 focuses on the professional environment and is directly related to professional engagement, which is concretized through: 1) Organizational communication 2) Professional cooperation 3) Professional reflection 4) Continuing professional development in the context of the digital environment Level 2 focuses on creating and sharing digital resources through the possibilities of: 

1) Selecting 2) Creating and modifying 3) Managing, protecting and sharing Level 3 focuses on managing and regulating the use of digital tools in learning and teaching. Level 4 builds on digital tools and strategies to improve evaluation, as well as the analysis of evidence and the realization of complete feedback on evaluation. Level 5 focuses on the use of digital tools to support learning, focusing on their full involvement, engagement, differentiation and personalization. Level 6 is concerned with the improvement of students' digital competence with a focus on their information and media literacy, meaningful communication, content creation, responsible use of information and communication technologies and digital resources, and problem solving through targeted use. Levels 2 through 5 represent the core of the pedagogical framework and they detail teacher competences to create and strengthen effective, publicly accessible and innovative learning strategies through digital tools [23].

documents.title: STEM Teachers’ Digital Competence: Different Subjects, Different Proficiencies
documents.snippet:
Areas 2 to 5, the core of the framework, detail the pedagogical and methodological aspects specific to the teaching process (designing, implementing, and assessing). Area 1 details the digital competences needed to engage with the professional working environment, and area 6 details the digital competences required to facilitate the development of students' digital competence. 

The DigCompEdu framework proposes a progression model that describes the different stages of digital competence development. These competence stages are expressed as proficiency levels, with A1 corresponding to the lowest and C2 to the highest. For each of the 22 competences, a proficiency descriptor is provided, exemplifying activities at each proficiency level. The descriptors provided by the framework were used to develop a self-reflection instrument, which is referred to ahead. 

The DigCompEdu framework and its related self-reflection instrument have been increasingly used to examine teachers' digital competence [23,24], but few studies have focused on these competences across different STEM subjects. The few available studies mostly pertain to single curricular subjects, small samples, or other contexts rather than school education. For instance, Rooy [25] concluded that experienced Australian biology teachers do incorporate technologies, however limited, in order to improve the quality of student learning. In Spain, Fraile, Peñalva-Vélez, and Lacambra [26] assessed the competence level of 43 schoolteachers in initial training and found it was low in content creation and problem solving. Those authors also highlighted the urgent need to purposefully incorporate relational and didactic aspects of digital technology integration in teacher education. 

While offering important insights, these studies fail to provide a more nuanced view of how digital competences are perceived by different teachers in STEM areas. Our study draws from a large sample, which constitutes a unique opportunity to focus on the differences across different STEM subjects.

Title: Assessing teachers’ digital competence in primary and secondary education: Applying a new instrument to integrate pedagogical and professional elements for digital education
Snippet: UNESCO's ICT CFT to their needs and educational context (Eurydice Report, 2019; UNESCO, 2018).

The International Society of Technology in Education (ISTE, 2018) developed the ISTE Standards for Teachers that provides guidelines for essential technology knowledge and skills. Furthermore, several countries have developed National frameworks combining items from more than one framework. For example, Estonia developed the Standards for Learning, Leading and Teaching in the Digital Age based on DigCompEdu and ISTE (2018), while Ireland developed the Digital Learning Framework which is based on DigCompEdu and UNESCO ICT CTF (Eurydice Report, 2019).

Another popular framework concerning the teachers' technological knowledge is the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), proposed by Mishra and Koehler (2006). The framework describes three basic components of knowledge during teaching and learning, namely technology, content, and pedagogy. TPACK describes the three main components of technological knowledge, pedagogical knowledge, and content knowledge as well as four intersectional components, namely, technological content knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, technological pedagogical knowledge, and technological pedagogical content knowledge (e.g., Schmid et al., 2020). Several studies have recently applied and (re)validated TPACK to assess the teachers' digital skills across different teaching stages and domains (e.g., Schmid et al., 2020).

Finally, several researchers used the International Computer Driving License (ICDL, 2018) to assess the teachers' digital competence, or developed web-based tools to efficiently integrate the framework in educational institutions (e.g., Idrizi et al., 2018). ICDL can be applied in any field of occupation and has been widely adopted by many countries and institutions to evaluate a person's knowledge on basic ICT concepts like computer basics, word processing and spreadsheets, typing skills, online essentials, online collaboration, image editing, security, presentation, and database.

Title: Exploring the nexus between digital competencies and digital citizenship of higher education students: a PLS-SEM approach
Snippet: Digital citizenship is then only possible on the basis of a particular kind of conduct, with empowered citizens taking responsibility for their own life outcomes, self-governing behaviour which requires them to invest time and energy in enterprising their own lives. To assess general digital competences, the DigComp framework includes content creation that is also relevant for digital citizenship (Findeisen & Wild, 2022). Digital content creation encompasses the process of generating and refining digital content, incorporating and integrating information and knowledge into an existing body of work, and simultaneously grappling with the enforcement of copyright and licencing, as well as providing clear and comprehensible instructions to computer systems. Digital content creation has emerged over the course of the last decade where users are encouraged to generate create their own content. The debate around citizenship and everyday creativity is more prominent in academic, as a glut of academic writing practices are associated with the creation. Consequently, students are encouraged to participate as digital content-creators and to design, create, make, remix and share their creative content using a range of digital tools and technologies (McGillivray et al., 2016;Thorpe & Gordon, 2012;Sevillano-Garc ıa & V azquez-Cano, 2015). In this study, we conceptualised digital content creation as HE students' ability to create and edit new content, integrate and re-elaborate previous knowledge and content. Based on this, the following hypothesis was formulated: H4: Digital content creation competence will positively influence higher education students' digital citizenship.

Title: Digital Competence of Educators (DigCompEdu): Development and Evaluation of a Self-assessment Instrument for Teachers' Digital Competence
Snippet: At the highest levels C1 and C2, teachers share their expertise with peers, experiment with innovative technologies and develop new pedagogical approaches. 

According to this approach, a teacher's general digital competences (as described in DigComp) is a prerequisite for developing the teacher-specific digital competences as described in DigCompEdu. Further prerequisites are the teacher's subjectspecific, pedagogical and transversal competences. 

Hence, DigCompEdu agrees with the TPACK framework published by Mishra and Koehler in 2006, which postulates that three knowledge areastechnological, pedagogical and content knowledgeneed to be effectively integrated for teachers to use digital technologies with added value in their teaching. However, where TPACK falls short of explaining how this connection is established, DigCompEdu aims to identify pedagogical and professional focus areas for the integration of technology into teaching and professional practice. To be able to supply such detail and still be applicable across all subjects and in a continuously changing technological landscape, the focus of DigCompEdu is clearly on the pedagogical element. DigCompEdu describes how technological competence (as described in DigComp) and subject-specific teaching competence (as described by curricula) can be pedagogically integrated by teachers to provide more effective, inclusive, personalised and innovative learning experiences to students. DigCompEdu furthermore acknowledges that to transform education in such a way a wider approach, including the professional environment and the integration of learning into the overall social and societal context is needed. Areas 1 and 6 cover these aspects.

Title: The effects of programming education planned with TPACK framework on learning outcomes
Snippet: In this model, content knowledge (CK), pedagogical knowledge (PK) and technological knowledge (TK) are the main information required for teacher development. Besides, when these areas are merged in pairs; Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK), Technological Content Knowledge (TCK) and Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) are formed three of which constitute the model: TPACK (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Pedagogical content knowledge is related to the learning approach and also choice of the material that best suits the course content (Angeli & Valanides, 2005;Cox & Graham, 2009). Technological Content Knowledge is about what technology should be used to teach successfully and Technological Pedagogical Knowledge is relative to choosing the most appropriate IT tool according to the determined learning / teaching needs (Hu & Fyfe, 2010). Mishra and Koehler (2006) defined TPACK as the basis for effective teaching by using technology. Besides, the meaning of TPACK includes; concept teaching using technology, pedagogical techniques that use technology through constructivist approaches to teach course content, knowledge of what makes concepts difficult or easy to learn and how these problems can be overcome by technology, knowledge of input and epistemological theories and knowledge of how technologies can be used to build on existing knowledge and lastly to develop new epistemologies or strengthen old ones (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). The ISTE (International Society for Technology in Education) (2007) standards, that 21st century students should have, include the "Digital Citizenship and Technology Practices and Concepts". Students who have "Digital Citizenship" competency give importance to the legitimacy and accuracy of the information they have reached on the internet. They have a positive attitude towards using technology that supports learning and cooperation. Moreover, students should be able to use technological applications, understand pertinent concepts and use new technology to learn via transferring their prior knowledge. One of the ways these standards can be referred to during instruction is producing a lesson plan developed with the TPACK framework. Bearing in mind the pedagogy; the methods that will be resorted to while presenting the input, the content itself and the technology that will be used is crucial in that sense.

The complex compound knowledge required by teachers falls within the intersection of all three areas. Besides, the meaning of TPACK includes; concept teaching using technology, pedagogical techniques that use technology through constructivist approaches to teach course content, knowledge of what makes concepts difficult or easy to learn and how these problems can be overcome by technology, knowledge of input and epistemological theories and knowledge of how technologies can be used to build on existing knowledge and lastly to develop new epistemologies or strengthen old ones (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). The ISTE (International Society for Technology in Education) (2007) standards, that 21st century students should have, include the "Digital Citizenship and Technology Practices and Concepts". Students who have "Digital Citizenship" competency give importance to the legitimacy and accuracy of the information they have reached on the internet. They have a positive attitude towards using technology that supports learning and cooperation. Moreover, students should be able to use technological applications, understand pertinent concepts and use new technology to learn via transferring their prior knowledge. One of the ways these standards can be referred to during instruction is producing a lesson plan developed with the TPACK framework. Bearing in mind the pedagogy; the methods that will be resorted to while presenting the input, the content itself and the technology that will be used is crucial in that sense.

Snippet: Due to the important differences in the frameworks and the diversity of aspects in which they differ, the comparative analysis is presented by contrasting them with DigCompEdu, because it is the most widely used and the most comprehensive. 

It is worth mentioning that in some frameworks the concept of dimensions is used, in others of areas and in others of competencies, so this is how it will be used in the following analysis. 

The dimensions used by the frameworks vary; however, some of these frameworks have been inspired by previous ones. For example, the DigCompEdu is considered the European Framework for Digital Competences, recognized by the European Union, which means that some of the dimensions are shared with the Spanish frameworks, such as DIGIGLO [19] and the Common Digital Teaching Competence Framework [38]. In these three frameworks, the competencies of digital content creation, security, and problem solving are identified. 

The Colombian framework is unique as it presents a dimension related to research, although some of the aspects related to it, such as creativity and innovation with digital technologies, are presented as a descriptor of digital competence in other frameworks. Similarly, the competence related to management exists as an independent dimension in the UNESCO ICT Competency Framework for Teachers, as well as in the Chilean and Colombian frameworks; in the other frameworks it is not present, although aspects related to other dimensions are mentioned. 

The only dimension common to all the frameworks Is the pedagogical dimension, referring in each case to the teacher's ability to make use of digital technologies in a way that supports students' learning processes.

Title: The HeDiCom framework: Higher Education teachers’ digital competencies for the future
